paragraphs.text: THE APOLOGETIC BOOK OF THE PRESBYTER

It is not my own ability or presumption, most blessed priests, but a most pressing and almost extreme necessity, as you yourselves recognize, that makes me appear as I now do. I was driven to it by injury, being not only the defender of my own faith but also the exposer of another's faithlessness.

For just as I am bound to clear myself for conscience' sake — and I mean not my own conscience but another's — so I am compelled, for the sake of faith and zeal, to point out with my finger the wolves found in the flock of sheep — and I mean not my own zeal but Christ's.

Yet since I am the least of all, I do not rashly presume anything. Necessity is laid on me to make known the injury I have suffered. Let those who did it be plain to all. For it is the will and ordinance of God that the evil which was being borne with patience should of necessity be exposed. Through the contentiousness of their fury, as they receive the fitting reward their error deserved, there should come about not only a branding of the most wicked doctrines but also an exposure of the persons who must be rebuked.

For the fathers have already published much against this wicked heresy in most approved writings, without naming the heretics: both the martyrs and confessors who have already gone to their rest, Cyprian, Hilary and Ambrose, and those for whom it is still needful even now to remain in the flesh, the pillars and foundations of the Catholic Church, Aurelius Augustine and Jerome.

And yet this abomination of most venomous doctrines has even now its living dead and its dead who live. For Origen and Priscillian and Jovinian, long since dead in themselves, live in these men, and not only live but also speak.

And now Pelagius and Caelestius, if they persist in these things as living dead men, behold, hiss openly against the Church, which is wretched, and, what is far more wretched, within the church. Like impious serpents licking their poisoned mouths with flickering tongues, they besiege the holy and most strongly fortified see into which they have subtly crept, and they frighten all the faithful from flying to that once most secure refuge in Zion. For the stench of their mouth, spread far and wide, has turned into death the fragrance of all those for whom it was a fragrance of life unto life.

Against this serpent and its suffocating breath the most blessed men whom we mentioned above have indeed compounded many and manifold sweet-smelling ointments from the scriptures, and to refresh the fevered hearts of the peoples they burn most fragrant incense together with the offering of prayer.

But it is too little to contend with an author who is left almost unnamed, and to temper the air infected with pestilential breath by setting opposites against opposites, unless the serpents themselves are dragged out into the open and trampled underfoot.

To protect their head alone, these men expose the rest of the body to cutting and injury. They think it no loss, so long as the one part of them that holds their many venomous tongues is kept free from danger, even if they are cut off in every limb. Does it seem enough to us, then, at least to content ourselves with tempering the stench, without moving them from the inner sanctuary?

— as though there could be any end to the fetid exhalation without an end to its source! And amid all this, does that testimony of Solomon not come to mind: "One builds, another tears down: what will either of them gain but toil?"

There stands also Goliath, monstrous in pride, swollen with carnal might, confident that he can do all things by himself with head and hand, and clad besides over his whole body in much bronze. Behind him he has his armor-bearer, who, though he does not fight himself, nevertheless supplies all the support of bronze and iron. And it is no wonder if Scripture, foreseeing this situation, fittingly declares: "The Philistines stood on the mountain on this side."

For the assailant of heresy is driven out of the Church, and the heretic is found being nursed in the Church's bosom; and for this reason the Holy Spirit declares that Israel stands on that side, the enemy on this. And this happens often. For King David too, a godly father, laid aside his royal attire and was driven from Jerusalem by his ungodly son, whereupon the tyrant Absalom at once entered.
So Goliath stands — alas! — on this side, that is, in the Church. And he not only stands but also issues his challenge, and for many days together he taunts holy Israel for its manifest fear.

Let no one, I beg you, most blessed priests, think that under cover of the figure of Goliath I am boasting of the name of David. It was you who wished me to share in your contest, so that I might come in as a helper, not as its instigator.

For I was living hidden in Bethlehem, an unknown and poor stranger — but why, wretch that I am, do I speak like this, perhaps to be branded with boasting again, since David himself was just such a man and came from there? So, I was living hidden in Bethlehem, entrusted by my father Augustine to learn the fear of the Lord sitting at the feet of Jerome. From there I came to Jerusalem when you summoned me; then, at the command of Bishop John, I went up together with you to your assembly.
There all of you asked my littleness to report faithfully and simply whatever I knew had been done in Africa concerning this heresy which Pelagius and Caelestius have sown.

I explained to your assembly as briefly as I could that Caelestius, who was already creeping into the honor of the presbyterate, had at Carthage, before many bishops sitting in judgment, been exposed, heard and convicted, had confessed, and had been condemned by the Church, and had fled from Africa;

that blessed Augustine, at the disclosure and request of Pelagius's own disciples, was replying most fully against Pelagius's book; and further, that I had in my hands a letter of the aforementioned bishop which he had recently sent to Sicily, in which he refuted many of the heretics' questions. You directed me to read it there and then, and I read it.

Thereupon Bishop John asked that Pelagius be brought in before them. Permission to bring him in was granted to John, both out of reverence for his fatherhood and for the benefit of the proceedings, since you believed that Pelagius could more properly be refuted by the bishop in person.

When Pelagius had been brought in, you all with one voice asked him whether he acknowledged having taught the things to which Bishop Augustine had replied. He answered at once: "And what is Augustine to me?" All cried out that one who blasphemed against the bishop through whose mouth the Lord had granted the healing of unity to the whole of Africa ought to be driven out, not only from that assembly but from the whole Church. Bishop John, however, at once ordered him — a layman, mark you, in an assembly of presbyters, and guilty of manifest heresy — to sit down in the midst of the Catholics, and then said:

"I am Augustine" — so that, by taking on the person of the absent man as though he were present, he might the more freely pardon on the authority of the one who was being insulted, and calm the feelings of those who were aggrieved.

We at once said to him: "If you take on the person of Augustine, follow Augustine's judgment." Then the same bishop said to all of us: "The things being read were said against others, but you think they should be brought forward as said about Pelagius. So if you have anything to say against Pelagius himself, bring it out."

Then, with your assent, I said: "Pelagius told me that he teaches that a man can be without sin and can easily keep the commandments of God, if he wishes." Pelagius answered in our hearing: "I cannot deny that I have said this and still say it."
I continued at once: "This the African synod condemned in Caelestius; this Bishop Augustine abhorred in his writings, as you have heard; this he now condemns in his reply to Pelagius's own writings;

this too blessed Jerome condemned in the letter he recently issued to Ctesiphon — Jerome, whose eloquence the whole West awaits like dew upon the fleece, for many heretics and their doctrines have already been stamped out by his attack — and he likewise refutes it in the book he is now writing, where the debate is set out in the form of a dialogue. For this is how to hold the slippery dragon on a hook, so that it cannot escape."

But Bishop John, paying no heed to any of this, tried to make us declare ourselves accusers with himself as judge. All answered again and again: "We are not his accusers; but we are informing you what your brothers, our fathers, have thought and decreed concerning this heresy, which a layman is now preaching publicly, so that he may not disturb the Church without your knowledge — your Church above all, to whose bosom we have fled."

He often tried, under the pretense of teaching, to draw us into some sort of declaration, saying that the Lord had said to Abraham, "Walk before me and be without blemish," and that Zechariah and Elizabeth were declared to be both righteous before the Lord, walking blamelessly in all the ordinances of the Lord. Several of us knew that he was bringing forward what Origen had said. I answered him: "We are sons of the Catholic Church. Do not demand of us, father, that we dare to be teachers above the teachers or judges above the judges. The fathers whom the whole Church throughout the world approves, and in whose communion you rejoice to remain, have decreed that these doctrines are damnable. It is right for us to obey what they approve. Why do you ask the sons what they think, when you hear what the fathers decree?"

At this he argued for a long time, while our statements suffered through the incompetence of an interpreter unknown to us. Again and again the eminent and devout men, the presbyters Passerius and Avitus and Domnus the former commander, corrected him as he mistranslated, or suppressed a great deal, or put one thing in place of another. So, with our proceedings, as I said, mostly either garbled or passed over in silence, Bishop John said:
"If he were saying that a man could do this without God's help, it would be most wicked and damnable; but since he adds that a man can be without sin, yet not without God's help, what do you say? Or

do you perhaps deny God's help?" I answered him: "With you and the aforementioned men as witnesses, who bear witness even now: anathema to anyone who denies the help of God. I certainly do not deny it, especially since I have argued against the heretics from just the opposite side."

Then, having seen through the judge and exposed the interpreter, we cried out that the heretic was a Latin and we were Latins, and that a heresy better known in the Latin regions should be examined by Latin judges. And since he, a single and suspect man, was thrusting himself forward almost shamelessly to judge — though we were not accusers — it became necessary for many to say: "No one can be at once heretic, advocate and judge."

After much else had been transacted, Bishop John pronounced his final decision, at last granting our request and purpose: that brothers and letters should be sent to blessed Innocent, the pope of Rome, and that all should follow whatever he decreed; but that in the meantime the heretic Pelagius should have silence imposed on him and keep quiet, and that our side should stop insulting a man convicted and self-confessed [?]. We all agreed to this decision. Thanks were given, peace was made, and after concluding with a prayer as a testimony of peace, we departed.

But now, forty-seven days later, on the first day of the Feast of the Dedication, I hurried, as I was accustomed to do when I was there, to pay my respects to Bishop John, and in place of the courtesy of a greeting I at once received from him the brand of a false charge. For he said to me: "Why do you come to me, you who have blasphemed?" He meant, I suppose, to be understood as saying: "Do not touch me, for I am clean and without sin." But I, conscious of nothing against myself, asked:
"When, or in whose hearing, or of what kind was the thing said that could be counted as blasphemy?" The bishop answered: "I heard you say that not even with God's help can a man be without sin."

I, most blessed priests, as you are witnesses, and the whole brotherhood, and besides them the holy men who out of love of the truth support this testimony, at once testified that no word of the kind the bishop now alleged I had spoken had ever come out of my mouth. And yet, as I chew over this unseemly and wretched falsehood by setting it out again and again, I may seem not so much to have proved my own innocence as to have exposed another man.

For let me grant that I said that statement, whatever it was: how did a Greek with no Latin understand a Latin speaker? Or, if he heard a sacrilegious word, why did he not at once rebuke the blasphemer, or, to act more gently, admonish him as a loving father admonishes a careless son to curb the license of dangerous speech?

On the contrary, after a long lapse of time he alone and by himself brought the accusation, bore the witness and pronounced the judgment, taking on every role in this wicked business on his own authority — and this although he had been carefully instructed by the gospel reading that our Lord Jesus was condemned on no other testimony than that of the chief priest.

On one side of me stood my brothers, on the other false brothers. Then in that same session there sat on one side with me the presbyters Avitus and Vitalis, on the other some unknown interpreter, and then men approved both by the world and by God, the presbyter Passerius and Domnus the former commander.
Both of these had been asked and brought in by your assembly, with Bishop John himself agreeing, so that they might kindly act as interpreters in view of their experience and good faith.

He himself, too, sat in your midst; and it is a wonder that in those circumstances he heard no less than he saw — how a word let fall could pass by so many adversaries, colleagues and hearers, and find its way into the uncomprehending ears of so knowing a listener.

But the heat of truth drives me on too hard: I am going beyond the bounds of my profession. It must rather be granted that the interpreter erred in speaking than that the bishop invented it in hearing, and is now looking for false witnesses to help him exact repayment for the favor he showed the heretics.

Yet no one ought to wonder any longer that false witnesses are sought out and come forward in Jerusalem from among priests and elders. The blood of Stephen cried this out, the banners of the Lord's cross signify it, and the injury they have stirred up even now makes it plain. But whether these things seem to have been rashly believed by the bishop, or maliciously invented, or ignorantly misheard, I commit to Christ the judge to examine.

Far be it from me ever, poor, sinful and unknown as I am, to dare to arraign a bishop, and especially the bishop of Jerusalem, before bishops. My simplicity and my tested integrity are enough for me before the most exalted Trinity of almighty God and before all his Catholic servants.

I call God as witness upon my soul, most blessed priests — and you know these same things and bear witness with me — that in that assembly of yours I uttered no blasphemy with my mouth, and did not say the words with which Bishop John has charged me, namely, that even with God's help a man cannot be without sin.

I wish [?] also to give satisfaction to the dispute of opinion, which is unknown to us: to you, so that you may not think that something was said by me even though you did not hear it, and so be troubled by doubtful testimony; and to the common people and to rumor, so that, unable to believe that a bishop could lie, they may not sin in another way by credulity against an innocent man. And who does not know, from this, who the instigators were in the accusation of Susanna and in the stoning of Naboth?

And lest anyone perhaps not know that in Jerusalem there has never been any lack either of silver to buy support or of soldiers' scourges for the shedding of Christian blood: now, since I consider myself free of this word, whatever it was — free by your good faith, free by my own conscience — I shall clear up the ambiguity of the word itself and try to examine how those who assert that we answered in this way appear to have framed the question themselves. Perhaps the very manner of their question will lay bare the secret of their doctrine, so that the darts, hurled back and striking with return wounds, may more surely punish the one who threw them.

For he says that we answered: "Not even with God's help can a man be without sin." If any man thinks this should be said in such a sense as to assert that God is powerless in the face of human weakness, and to suspect that anything in all creation, in heaven, on earth or under the earth, is impossible to God's omnipotence, I would say that such a man is not only, in my judgment, a blasphemer to be abhorred and anathematized, but deserves either to be condemned by divine fire after the example of Nadab and Abihu, or to be swallowed alive by the opening earth and plunged into hell, like Dathan and Abiram in their destruction.

For both of these, in the presumption of their hearts, detracted from the power of God: the former when they offered strange fire, as though God had need of it; the latter when, resisting Moses, they doubted that they could be brought into the land of promise.

God can do all things, and what he wills he can always do: as powerful in making things from nothing as he is ready to perfect what has been made. For whenever he wills, the power to do it lies within himself. This the grace granted according to the spirit confesses; this the law written according to the letter attests; this the natural law perceives in all things; this the most orderly motion of the world displays.
For which of the Gentiles would dare to say otherwise, when they always have before their eyes the distinct elements of heaven, earth and sea?

What Jew could suspect it, if even a little knowledge of the law given through Moses has reached him, since he recognizes and believes what is written: that when the waves of the Red Sea were parted, the depths lay bare and offered a safe path through the sea to those who went on foot

as on dry land; that the Jordan was divided and its waters turned back and flowed toward their source; that Elijah, mortal in body, was carried up by the fire of a fiery chariot and not harmed; or that Habakkuk, laden with the food he had prepared, so that he might serve a meal to a fasting righteous man among hungry beasts, was, as the common edition relates, carried in a moment of the day from Judea to Babylon and immediately brought back?

What Christian would admit it into his heart, even in the smallest atom of thought, when he knows that Lazarus, four days dead, his limbs stinking and already dissolving within their skin, sprang forth to the devoted service of the Lord; when he has read that a man blind from birth, and already of age, became strong with eyes either suddenly made or restored;

when he has found that winds, waves and storms, and the elements warring with one another, grew calm on hearing the command of the Lord's rebuke; when he believes that Peter, heavy with the burden of the flesh and soon to deny the Lord three times, walked with suspended steps over the swelling waves?

Therefore I think that all men, whether those endowed with excellent faith and wisdom or those otherwise disposed, revere, believe and confess this: that God can do all things. For he is called almighty by all creation alike precisely because he can do all things. And it is God alone who says: "These things are impossible with men." And elsewhere he teaches, saying: "Without me you can do nothing."

So he who can do all things can do all things in man. Why then is earth and ashes so proud as to say "man can," when it is God who can? The apostle cries out: "By his grace I am what I am, and his grace in me was not wanting, but I labored more abundantly than all of them: yet not I, but the grace of God with me." Why, rash presumer, do you fix your eyes on his saying "with me"?

Notice that he said "not I" first. Between these two phrases, "not I" and "with me," therefore, stands the grace of God, to which truly belong both the willing and the accomplishing according to good will, and yet with the will of man. That is why he who had said "not I" was confident enough to say "with me."

So the grace of divine power works in the will of man, and it is that grace which has given the very willing. Thus man's conscience confesses, so that he says "not I"; God's grace bestows, so that he can say "with me."

The apostle cries out: "By the grace of God I am what I am." For he remembered the Lord preaching: "No one comes to me unless the Father draws him"; and again elsewhere: "And I am with you always, to the end of the age." And in another place he speaks thus of the Holy Spirit: "It is to your advantage that I go away; for if I do not go away, the Comforter will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you."

Wretched man, by the truth of God's verdict! The Father draws you, the Son is with you, and so is the Spirit the Comforter, and with the divine majesty all around you like this you dare to say: "By the help of God's grace, indeed, but by my own capacity I am what I am"!

For now, after this correction, which only keeps company with your old error, you assert: "Man can be without sin with God's help." Yet in your book, which you entitled Testimonies, this very statement is written as follows: that man can be without sin and easily keep God's commandments, if he wills.

No grace of God is named there, no help, however often you say of the grace of God: "I did not deny it just because I did not mention it; rather, I should be taken to have said it, because I did not deny it." As if Susanna were to be believed to have confessed adultery because she did not deny it when others accused her, or the Lord Jesus had approved the testimony of the false witnesses because he was silent!

But if, among you people, not denying is the same as saying, and keeping silent is the same as shouting, then David prays in vain: Set a guard, O Lord, over my mouth, and a door to enclose my lips. And in vain do I too prove by witnesses and testimony that I did not say what I am accused of, if someone else could hear what my words did not say.

But I grant that you may think what you never said should be taken as said. What are we to make of the fact that we find your words at odds with your meaning, so that they do not hold together, their joints clashing, and that the very page cannot hold words that conflict with one another? For you write that man can be without sin and easily keep God's commandments, if he wills; and then, as the most blessed father Jerome showed about this same statement in the letter he wrote to Ctesiphon, at the very end, as if waking from a very heavy sleep, you add: "not without God's help."

Here the truth itself opposes you and protests. Why, out of disdainful pride and squeamish modesty, do you keep God's help in your mouth as something you do not need, since you think everything is easy for you?

You honour me with the tips of your lips, but your heart is far from me. A task that is easy for one does not need two to do it, and the grace of the Godhead puts itself forward in vain where a man declares that he can do the thing easily if he wills. You said that the commandments are easy for one who wills; but I go further and maintain that you are saying even difficult ones are fulfilled.

Yet however you claim that man can do it, you charge the Lord with envy, as though by adding his help he were trying to claim for himself what man could have accomplished alone by his own will. Either take "if he wills" away from man and ascribe to grace what he can do, or, since you credit man with being able when he wills, drop this feigned, flattering and incoherent share given to grace, and openly profess the blasphemy that comes out of the abundance of your heart.

But it is not my part to investigate these matters more broadly, especially since the most blessed fathers Augustine and Jerome have given the western provinces the fullest proof that this heresy stands convicted. Let me return to the question proposed above, which I took up not because I was confident in my own talent but because I was stirred by an injury.

You say that in this world man can be without sin with God's help. You say "man can"; I say God can. The flame raging inside the furnace did not harm the three young men. Which of them was able to do what was done against nature: they themselves, or the fourth in their midst, who was like the Son of God?

The leper cries out: Lord, if you will, you can make me clean, making the will manifest through the power and confirming the will through the power. For he alone is the one for whom, when he wills, the power is at hand. The blind came to him, praying to be given sight, and Jesus said to them: Do you believe that I can do this? The Lord Christ judges anyone who believes that the Son of God can do these things worthy of the highest reward for faith; and our Briton is confident that he himself can, as soon as he wills! To the faithful paralytic the Lord says: Take heart, son:

your sins are forgiven you. And now a new master, a minister of tables, has dared instead to take the remission of sins for granted on the strength of his own capacity, and does not wait to hear it from the Lord! The scribes, not understanding the truth, murmur and say: Who can forgive sins but God alone? And this man judges that sins are wiped out when he does not know that God has forgiven them!

Look at you, puffed up by the spirit of your flesh, as if there were nothing above you, proudly glorying in free will and saying: "I am a sinner because I will it; I sin as long as I will it; but when I will otherwise, I can be without sin." When you say "I sin when I will," that is true, because what you have not done in deed you have done in thought. Again, "when I will, I do not sin" is hard and difficult, to be sure, and not always within everyone's reach, but there is still no doubt that it can happen at times.

But for someone who has once sinned to be able to be without sin is impossible, except by the grace of baptism alone, where it is said in the person of the Lord: Your sins are forgiven you. This I am persuaded to believe, because I am allowed to hear it. But "therefore I can be without sin," at least in this corruption in which we live, I do not accept, I do not presume, I do not dare.

For if David prays to God, Against you alone have I sinned and done evil before you, and if, according to John's Revelation, the dead are to be judged by the sins they committed before God, by what is written in the books, receiving according to their works, why should I presume to pass my own judgment on myself, when I know that I too am to be judged?

Or, if those sacred books, which will never be opened except at the judgment, record the good and evil of our life alike, to supply the judgment with its weighing, how can we know that sins have been wiped out without examination in this life and before death, when we read that they are to be brought forth not only after death but even after the resurrection?

It was in my power to sin; it is not in my power to be freed from sin. To pray is mine; to be absolved is not mine. When I gave myself over to sin, I became the slave of the accuser and a defendant before the judge. Because I have first offered the support of constant prayers, I can take hope from the good judge; but I cannot claim an innocent conscience without fear before the sentence is pronounced.

For the apostle says: Do not judge anything before the time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts; and then each will receive praise from God. Otherwise, if it is in man's power to make himself free from his sin, either Christ is not the judge or he is judge to no purpose.

But you say: "I spoke of man being without sin in this sense: when the sinner groans, then he will be saved, that is, then he will begin to share in salvation." Yet he will not be without sin at once. For when the Lord entered the house of Zacchaeus, who believed, he said: Today salvation has come to this house. Surely, if one man believed, the whole household was not at once without sin, even though at that moment, when the master of the house believed, the beginning of salvation entered it?

For David too groaned when he had sinned, and although he was granted to hear that his offence was forgiven, yet long afterwards he atoned for that very sin by exile and much disgrace. So it plainly appears that a penalty was paid in the present and forgiveness promised for the future, and that by this God showed great mercy to the groaning sinner, letting him purge by a temporary chastisement a sin that deserved death.

It is said to Ananias about Paul, when he complained fearfully of Paul's persecution: I will show him how much he must suffer for my name. Thus Paul was to be loosed in the very place where he had bound by persecuting Christ, and soon, suffering for Christ and afflicted even to death, he was to stand forth glorified in the resurrection. So it is, since mercy and truth always go before the face of God: if in time one who groans offers the voluntary sacrifice of a troubled spirit and a contrite heart, so that truth is done in mercy, then at the end mercy is preferred to judgment.

The Lord Christ, who will come in the glory of God the Father, is believed in and hoped for as the one who will judge the living and the dead, from whose sight, as Scripture testifies, heaven and earth will flee. And there are men who, out of ignorance, not to say out of conscience, do not consider themselves subject to the judge who is to come, and do not tremble at the coming of the Lord and the brightness of his splendour, when the elements are burning and the world is perishing!

I fear they will be among those of whom the Lord forewarns: For many will say on that day (men, that is, of that fleshly arrogance by which they led others astray, righteous not so much before God as in their own eyes) Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name and do great mighty works in your name? And then I will swear to them and say: I never knew you; depart from me, workers of iniquity.

Through the prophet David it is said in the person of Christ: Lord, who will dwell in your tabernacle, or who will rest on your holy mountain? He who walks without stain and works righteousness. This is really to say: he who can be, and is, without sin.

For the Lord himself says of himself: The prince of this world is coming, and finds nothing of his in me. What, then, belongs to the devil? Sin, without doubt. For the devil is a liar from the beginning, whereas my Lord is the one who speaks truth in his heart and has worked no deceit with his tongue.

As Scripture testifies, a great and mighty angel cries out in heaven: Who is worthy to open the book and loose its seals? And when no one, either in heaven or on earth or under the earth, could open the book or look

into it, John weeps much and mourns, because out of the whole of rational creation no one was found worthy to open the book so as to see it. One of the elders consoles the weeping John and says: Do not weep, John. Behold, the lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has conquered, so as to open the book and loose its seals. What book is this, I ask, which no one [?] to receive from the hand of him who lives for ever, except the one who walks without stain and works righteousness?

It is not enough that he is without stain, not enough that he is a lamb, unless he was also slain, unless he had crowned the purity of his life with the witness of his passion, having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God: no doubt the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and piety, the spirit of the fear of the Lord. What, then, is this book? The book of judgment, I believe. For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son. Alas! I am forced to say what I shuddered even to think.

See now: Pelagius too, who has dared to declare that he is without stain and sin, consequently thinks himself worthy to receive the book and the judgment. The next step is for him to say, "I have power to lay down my life and to take it up again," and to prepare himself to share Christ's throne.

Wretched man, who does not understand instead that he is preparing himself to be the forerunner of the coming of Antichrist, who, when he is revealed, exalts himself above all that is called God or is worshipped, just like this man, who is already comparing himself with the only Son of God so as to make himself his equal.

The Lamb of God, the Son of God, displays the marks of his passion in order to receive the book from the Father's hand, judging his victory complete only in death and resurrection; and my "sinless one" assures us that the perfection of a stainless life can come to him while he eats, drinks and sleeps!

After a forty-day fast the devil tempted our Lord Jesus three times and, three times defeated, left him; yet he did not leave him for ever, but only for a time, intending to return more fiercely, even to the death of the cross [?]. And our "passionless one," having conquered the temptations together with their author, as he imagines, is confident that he can no longer be tempted or troubled!

That perfect Lamb, who not only has no sins but even takes away the sins of the world, and who has seven horns and seven eyes, could not drive off the tempter so thoroughly that he would not return; and this mutilated fellow of ours, with his smooth brow and his two eyes, thinks he needs no defence on his head, since he takes for granted that he has the capacity in the flesh!

Wretched man, who, according to the Gospel, would perhaps rather have no sin if he were blind! But perhaps, since the seven eyes are the seven spirits, he boasts that he abounds in all of them, and that his inner man flourishes with the accumulated powers of sevenfold grace, especially since he prides himself on just as many headings of his doctrines.

So it may be that by his own judgment he thinks himself filled with the spirit of wisdom, above all because he says that God's commandments are easy; amply supplied with the spirit of understanding, by which he foreknows and proclaims that all sinners, together with the impious, are to be condemned to eternal fire;

rich in the spirit of counsel, by which he warns that evil must not even be thought of; mighty in the spirit of might, by which he affirms that man can be without sin; puffed up with the spirit of knowledge, by which he holds that no one can be without sin unless he has knowledge of the law;

overflowing with the spirit of piety, by which he teaches that an enemy is to be loved like a friend, forgetting that he himself said an enemy is in no way to be trusted; distinguished by the spirit of the fear of God, by which, waking at last after a long drunken stupor, he adds that man can be without sin, "not without God's help."

And by these steps of presumption, I think, he does not fear to climb, carried so high as to say that the Holy Spirit, full with the perfection of his power, descended wholly upon him and remained, in the likeness of Christ;

although this was given by God the Father to him alone, to whom he also gave the name that is above every name, who alone is without sin and walks without stain, with whom the very ointment of sanctification abides. But we run after the fragrance of his ointments, and meanwhile, with the Lord going before us, we catch upon ourselves the sweet breaths of life from the breeze of the life-giving air.

But you say: "Why do you assail me with such an insult? Why do you burden me with the odium of so arrogant a statement? Would I, a servant, dare to compare myself with my Lord? Would I, who am earth and ashes, set myself beside the Word of God? Should I, who am subject to death, be called equal to the conqueror of death?"

Well said, to be sure, O condemned wickedness: you bear witness to God and humble yourself in words, but your meaning cries out otherwise in your pages. You say that man can be without sin; I repeat it again and again.

The man who can do this is Christ: either claim the name or give up your confidence. God granted this to one alone, and to none but the firstborn among many brothers. So it is handed down by the catholic faith, and so we hold.

Indeed our Lord warned the unbelievers: I have come in my Father's name, and you did not receive me; another will come in his own name, and perhaps you will receive him. Either follow with us the one in whom we sinners believe, the one who is without sin and is likewise the Only-begotten, or, if you are that other, confess it.

He is the Lord Jesus, who, having conquered death and triumphed over the devil, ascended on high, led captivity captive, and gave gifts to men; of his fullness we have all received, as the apostle teaches: But to each one of us grace was given according to the measure of Christ's gift.

And the same teacher of the Gentiles writes to the Romans: For by the grace given to me I say to everyone among you: do not think more highly than you ought to think, but think with sober judgment, each according to the measure of faith that God has apportioned.

Then he declares to the Corinthians: There are varieties of graces, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of workings, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of ministries, but the same God who works all things in all. And after listing many graces and powers, he adds: But all these are worked by one and the same Spirit, who distributes to each as he wills.

Then, by comparison with the members of the human body, he shows that the body of the Church's unity is brought together out of unlike ways of working into one harmony of perfection. He proves that there is no member at all that does not need the help and support of another, while the Lord himself is set as the head, in whom all understanding and all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden.

So he has also given us understanding, by which we might know what the Word is in Christ Jesus, in whom the whole fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily; on whom, according to John's testimony, the Holy Spirit descended and remained, declaring him to be the Lord.

Therefore, if no one has anything except one who asks it of you [?], and no one receives except according to distribution and measure, and whoever has received needs another's help to keep it, by what madness, I ask, does someone who is not sufficient even in his own single part promise himself the fullness?

The evangelist testifies of the Lord: He was the true light, which enlightens every man coming into this world. But the Lord says to his apostles: You are the light of this world. There, in the Lord alone, is the whole light, because it is true light; here, in all the apostles, there is light indeed, but light from the light that is whole.

And if this is so with the apostles, in whose election the whole body of the Church was taken up, what can we (we, I mean, as individuals) appear to be after them, except, as the apostle Peter says, ignorant men who simply believe through faith in the word of the gospel and the prophets, as in a lamp shining in a murky place?

As though we ourselves had also been enlightened, we are urged to have burning lamps in our hands, prepared in good works; yet, worn down by temptations of many kinds, they are always in danger, both from their own failing and from blows struck by others. Hence the Lord too says in the Gospel: And if the very light that is in us is darkness, how great will the darkness be?

But I grant that this light, however small it is, may remain with unfailing strength to the end, that is, that it does not lose that gift of special grace which it received. (Otherwise, where the fullness of light is present in the whole, no darkness remains; and by darkness I mean the darkness of folly that comes from the filth of sin.) What if it is a fitting reckoning that however much light is lacking, just so much darkness remains?

Moreover, it is extremely hard for darkness to hold no stumbling block. A man placed in a measure of light and amid the remnants of darkness, who wills the good but does not escape evil, must both have help at hand and not be without sin.

If this seems obscurely put to anyone, let him take an example from human life. Two individuals have different gifts: one is humble in silence, the other persuasive in teaching. If the one who loves silence is asked, as may happen, to give an account of the faith, do you think he will not stumble at all in arguing? Or if the one entrusted with the task of teaching is rebuked for arrogance, do you think he will not take on some pretence in his humility?

Or do you think it easy for the simple man to be free of buffoonery, the cheerful man of idle talk, the zealous man of anger, the patient man of negligence, the gentle man of sloth, the learned man of boasting, the submissive man of envy, not to mention the desire for vainglory, which is the darkness that hangs over all good works generally?

If this is understood piously and devoutly, let each of us make a comparison, so as to condemn himself by setting the better man above him rather than justify himself by looking down on the lesser. In this way he will at last join the members to one another, especially if, with one charity surrounding them as skin surrounds the bones, and their needs joining them like sinews, a man aware of himself understands that the very grace he has is a gift, not a debt, and glories in the Lord for what he has received rather than being angry over what he has not received.

For although by nature we were children of wrath because of our offence, we were made children of mercy because of the Lord's clemency, though we deserved nothing but condemnation. Let us not heap complaints on the Lord over what we have not received, but for what we have received let us return thanks and glory to him alone, our Creator and Redeemer, the Lord Jesus Christ, whom God set forth as a propitiation in his blood, so that at his name every knee should bow, in heaven, on earth and under the earth; whom all flesh will see judging in that foretold power, and whom every tongue will confess.

Hence the apostle also says: Therefore we strive, whether absent or present, to please him. For we must all be made manifest before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive what is due for what he did in the body, whether good or evil. And elsewhere: For we shall all stand before the judgment seat of God.

The apostle Paul said that even he would stand before the judgment seat of God and, with everyone else, render account for what he had done in the body; yet Pelagius, on the contrary, confidently dares to say: "I so complete the whole of perfection in the flesh that I hope for nothing from the judge's goodness."

On that day the righteous, hearing from the judge of the glories of their works, will still ask as though they did not know: Lord, when did we see you and do these things for you? And this man of ours, so very learned in the law, knows on what day, at what hour, at what moment he will enter that final seat of the most complete holiness, beyond which there is no other!

Or perhaps he protests and says: "These reproaches of madness, not to say of pride, would rightly be heaped on me if I said that a man can be without sin without help. But in fact I assert the help of God, to whom nothing is difficult. Or do you perhaps deny God's help?"

I yield to your slander for a little while. Then, while I seem to be uncovering in myself what I wish to convict in you, we shall both be found out together: I shall be shown the clearer in my defence, and you the more exposed in your confusion.

This has always been my faithful and undoubted conviction. God supplies his help not only in his body, which is the Church, on which he bestows special gifts of his grace because of the faith of believers. He also supplies it to all the nations in this world, because of his long-suffering and eternal mercy.

He does not do this, as you assert together with your disciple Celestius, whose hidden nature of impious doctrines has already been crushed at the African synod, by bestowing one grace on all in general, consisting only in natural good and in free will. Rather, he supplies it specifically and daily, through seasons, through days, through moments, through instants, to all and to each. For Scripture says: "who makes his sun rise on the good and the evil." But perhaps you answer:

"Nature, once well arranged, keeps its order, and so God, having established the courses of the elements once and for all, acts from then on only in that he made them." What then do you think of the part of the saying that follows: "He gives rain on the just and the unjust"? Surely he who gives, gives when he wills and where he wills, whether by administering the order he has established or by pouring out his own bounty.

And in case the madness of your impiety leads you to plan to make even this void, hear the prophet bearing witness to this truth: "He who calls the waters of the sea and pours them out on the face of the earth, the Lord is his name." And what shall I say of the true hope of the human race, since everyone who ploughs ploughs in hope? Yet to hope is not a matter of one's own ability but of another's bounty.

When someone has sown, and the farmer has hidden the scattered seed in the bosom of the earth, he has nothing more to do but lift his eyes to heaven. He prays, not to the earth to which he entrusted the seed, but to God in whom he has believed, that God will make his labours fruitful with the early or the late rain. And to apply a spiritual testimony to common use as well: "neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but God who gives the growth."

Measure, then, how much I rejoice in the help of God by this: I maintain that it is supplied in every particular even to the nations. This is so that it may be plain to us whom we must beware of to the end, and whom we must call upon without ceasing.

The devil is asked by the Lord: "Where have you come from?" And he answered: "I am here, having gone around the earth and travelled through all that is under heaven." I ask you: does this busy activity of the devil come from good will or from evil? You must admit that it comes entirely from evil, as his next demand also shows.

This appearance of the devil took place in the time of Job, that is, in the time of Moses. Certainly there was then no Judea, no Jerusalem, no Church throughout the world. The whole Gentile world did not yet have knowledge of God. Yet even then the devil was going around the earth, travelling through everything under heaven, driven by the unceasing zeal of his malice to seduce and destroy the human race.

So when you see that the devil's wickedness bent itself so hard to destroying men who did not know God, do you believe that no grace of God was there to guard them? Or perhaps you think it was said in vain: "The earth is the Lord's and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it."

But indeed, so that you may prove more plainly that God's help is present in every particular and for every person, see: the devil himself, while he testifies about the whole world, is questioned about one man. "Have you considered," says God, "my servant Job, that there is no one like him on earth?"

The Lord knows each one individually, and so does the devil: the one by the power of his nature, the other by the toil of wickedness; the latter in order to tempt, the former in order to prove. Job is praised by the Creator while the adversary contradicts. The Lord wishes to judge the work of the man, a work which he himself works in him. But even the devil confesses God's help, for he says: "Have you not hedged about what is outside his house and what is inside it?"

At the enemy's demand God strips his servant through temptation, but he does not leave him naked. He takes away his substance and gives grace. "Behold," he says, "all that he has I give into your hand, but do not touch him himself." This is too little for the envious one. He rages and tries to bring death. But in turn God's dispensation is adjusted, while grace is not withdrawn: the prey the robber demanded is granted to him, and then he is made guardian of his own prey. For it is said to him: "Behold, I hand him over to you; only guard his life."

Let no one infer from this that the devil labours only to seduce the soul while it is in the body, and not also to tear it out of the body itself. He would do so if the protection of a merciful God did not defend man in his wounds and weakness, and did not always go out to meet every attempt of the devil's snares.
You now have, I think, sufficient proof of cooperating grace even among the nations. Receive also a clear indication of that chief gift which he bestows specially on the Church, his body.

The apostle Paul writes to the Corinthians: "I give thanks to my God always for you because of the grace of God that has been given you in Christ Jesus, for in him you have been made rich in everything, in all speech and in all knowledge, just as the testimony of Christ has been confirmed in you, so that you lack nothing in any grace." And again: "Therefore, having been justified by faith, let us have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have access by faith into this grace in which we stand and boast."

Hence the apostle Peter also admonishes, saying: "receiving the end of your faith, the salvation of souls. Concerning this salvation the prophets inquired and searched, who prophesied of the grace of God that was to come to us." From this it is most plainly declared that God's help is lacking to no one, especially since the seducer presses on and weakness is within.

The slander of the blind accuser who said, "Perhaps you deny God's help?" has been confounded and refuted. But we have mentioned Job, and in the testimony above he was described by the Lord's own words as a man without crime, a true worshipper of God, keeping himself from all evil.

For it is very often repeated by us, as proof that a man can be without sin, that there has been such a man: that is, that Job was called by God's testimony a man without crime and true, and that Zacharias is shown in the Gospel to have been approved as blameless.

The Lord said of Job, "a man without crime"; did he say "without sin"? For sin is conceived in thought, but crime is revealed only by an act. And being "blameless" is a matter of the knowledge and judgment of men. They can readily see gentleness in a face, but they do not know the wars of the heart.

Hence Paul too confidently commands: "For a bishop must be without crime." And elsewhere he gives a general testimony to the Corinthians and asserts: "so that you lack nothing in any grace, as you await the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ, who will also confirm you to the end without crime."

See: those whom Paul by his testimony confirms to be without crime to the end, he soon rebukes in the same letter, writing: "It is already altogether a fault in you that you have lawsuits among yourselves." Under one heading and of the same persons, we find "without crime" and we find "a fault." So he shows that when you see someone called without crime, it does not at once follow that he is declared to be without fault.

For the Lord Jesus also said: "John came neither eating nor drinking." And again it is written: "His food was locusts and wild honey." Are we to conclude from one or the other that either John did not eat or the Lord was mistaken? On the contrary, there is truth in both. John took some food to sustain his flesh, and yet the Lord spoke truly of John, since he ate neither with others nor what others ate. Here the Lord shows that he and the holy Scriptures often set forth the judgments of men while the knowledge of God is kept hidden.

Therefore it is reverently understood that whenever Scripture calls someone both just and blameless, this is said according to the measure of the time and the judgments of men. It is not said according to that final judgment of God, to which the conscience of all is subject and which the tongue of all shall confess.

Understand clearly, then, that by the provident counsel of God, Job's being declared just and his being allowed to suffer in the flesh brought about the confounding of the arrogant devil. Thus, while the man was praised for the honour of his Creator, with the Lord himself approving him, the angel who sought to turn aside the brand of faithlessness might be punished.

But God also took care that in healing his servant he should not deal him a heavier blow, and should not wound the soul by caring for the flesh. That is, after blessed Job had overcome so great a temptation and had had everything doubled and restored to him, he was not to be lifted up into pride and fall into the judgment of the devil. So he is admonished about his hidden faults. Though he was praised outwardly for his righteousness, he was to know that inwardly he ought to be subject to the one by whom he was kept. For the Lord says to him:

"Who is this who hides counsel from me, keeping words in his heart, and thinks he is hidden from me? Gird up your loins like a man. I will question you, and you shall answer me. Where were you when I founded the earth? Tell me, if you have understanding."
And after much correction by teaching, or teaching by correction, Job answered the Lord and said: "Why am I judged, admonished and rebuked by the Lord, hearing such things when I am nothing?"

Such also was Zacharias, a blameless man, worthy of honour among men, worthy of the testimony of the Scriptures. Some swelling of pride, I think, was already stirring in him because of this, and he was beginning to trust his reputation more than his conscience. So he is charged with the mark of unbelief by the angel who rebukes him, and is punished with a temporary silence.

Hence Paul too says: "Therefore let anyone who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall." And as a pattern for men he declares of himself: "I chastise my body and bring it into subjection, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become reprobate." So to call someone without crime and blameless is not a testimony to perfection but an example of conduct.

Wherever Scripture speaks of the "undefiled," as when David says, "Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord," I take sound doctrine to teach this: truly blessed are those who are undefiled in the way, that is, who walk in the truth with perfect faith and do not turn aside into heretical perversity, either to the right or to the left.

The way is Christ, who leads to the Father through the Holy Spirit. Whoever, then, without stain or leprosy, and not violated by those whose speech creeps like a cancer, hears, believes and understands the glory of the venerable Trinity, stands blessed and undefiled in faith.

This is why it is also said to Abraham: "Walk before me and be without stain." Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness, so that he might be in what he believed: he saw and rejoiced. He is therefore necessarily admonished to be perfect and without stain, since he was made father of many nations in faith and the bosom of the faithful, so that all of us who hope in God may be at rest with faithful Abraham.

"Blessed are the undefiled in the way," it is written; for we walk by faith, not by sight. But if you wish to hear about the undefiled man that David seeks in prayer, lay aside your vain confidence in your own ability. Prostrate yourself in prayer, join your prayer to the prophet's, and weep with him, saying: "Who understands his faults? Cleanse me from my hidden faults, O Lord, and spare your servant from those of others. If they do not have dominion over me, then I shall be undefiled."

Wretched man that I am, when shall I avoid the faults I do not yet understand? Peter loves Christ and never turns aside from that love. On the Lord's testimony to his love he is at one moment established as the rock of the Church's foundation, and at another disgraced with the name of Satan. He always does one and the same thing, yet at one moment it is said to him: "Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven"; and at another this is thrust upon him: "You do not have in mind the things of God, but the things of men."

The apostle was chosen for his love and confounded for his love, and his sin came from excessive love. For when the Lord announced his passion, Peter in the impatience of love had said: "Be merciful to yourself, Lord; this shall not happen to you."

O misery of the miserable! If Peter sinned in some way by loving Christ, who understands his faults? The prophet cries out, and he cries out in the Holy Spirit. He is the one of whom the Lord had said, "My hand will help him, and my arm will strengthen him, and the enemy shall gain nothing against him." Mark what he cries: "Cleanse me from my hidden faults, O Lord."

Consider David, chosen according to God's heart. God promised that he would do all his will, anointed him king, and endowed him with the sanctification of the prophetic spirit. Yet David, astonished at how sins had crept in on him unawares, cries to the Lord and implores to be cleansed from his hidden faults. And in another place the Lord says to him: "You shall not build a house for my name, because you are a man of war and have shed blood." It is as though God really could not wash away all his stains and cleanse him enough to make him a worthy man for a worthy work!

David is not cleansed until his death. Instead, when his son is preferred to him for building the temple, he condemns himself. And yet Goliath with his armour-bearer slanders me, asking why the Lord should not do in him what he has never done in the world!

Ecclesiastes too says: "There is nothing new under the sun, nor can anyone say: See, this is new; for it has already existed in the ages before us." Yet the teacher of new doctrines asserts: "What has never been done can be done! Do not ask whether it has been, when you do not doubt that it can be."

God willed that a house be built for his name, but on condition that only an innocent and truly undefiled man should build it. Two kings are chosen for this with all strength, each of them with help, and protection is promised to both. For God says of David: "My truth and my mercy shall be with him." And of Solomon he testifies: "I have chosen him to be my son, and I will be a father to him."

Of these two, one prepares the temple of the Lord and the other builds it. The old man prepares it; the young man completes it. For it is fitting that a holy man should build the holy temple of the Lord. The old man prepares, as I said, but only after he had, as it were, ceased to sin; the young man completes it, but almost before he had begun to sin. The one sinned before, the other afterwards. The one, because of much sin, was not found worthy to build; the other, by sinning much, abandoned what he had built.

Amid all this, the holy ordinance wonderfully arranged things so that, between two ages of life, it found for a limited time what could not be permanent in man. Each of them at some time did not sin, yet neither could be without sin, so that God may be true and every man a liar, as it is written: "Vain are the sons of men, the sons of men are liars in the balances."

David and Solomon certainly had the grace and help of God, yet David could not attain sinlessness, nor could Solomon keep it. And the son of Jovinian hopes that almighty God will change so great an order of things for him and his disciples! And if perhaps it does not happen, will he accuse God of being unable?

"A man can be without sin," he says, "yet with the help of God." What shall I do? For the moment I will put up with this new patch sewn onto an old garment, until a worse tear exposes the falsity of this wretched correction. For, against the guidance of the truth that speaks, I grant that when he said "a man can, if he wills," he may be taken to have said "a man can, with the help of God."

Now at last I must call my discourse back, as it were, to the beginning of the proposition. Setting aside for a while the pain of the injury done to me, I must return, with the reverence proper to debate, to the loftiness of the Head.

For our Head is Christ Jesus. As the apostle says, God set him forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood, to show his righteousness because of the remission of former sins, in the forbearance of God, and to show his righteousness at this time, so that he himself might be just and the one who justifies whoever has the faith of Jesus.

So the propitiator through faith in his blood, set forth to show and to model righteousness, is himself the mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus. Of him John, led almost into that very inaccessible light, exclaims: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him."

And a little later, having set out the truth of the divine work, he adds: "And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us; and we saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth." He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth. Like a lamb before its shearer, he did not open his mouth when he was scourged, crucified and put to death. He tamed the sting of death, rose from the dead, and, leading captivity captive, ascended into heaven.

He is the only-begotten in the Father and the firstborn among many brothers, in whom all the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily. This, then, is the Lord Christ; this, I say, is the Son of God, who in the power and glory of the Father created in the beginning, redeemed in the middle, and will also judge at the end.

So, after founding the whole creation, which came into being according to his will, he set a measure on the things he had ordered. What had been made rational was to subsist by reason. And what he had endowed with free will he restrained by the law of a commandment, lest it run off into a licence that leads to perdition. This was so that the creature

might acknowledge its Creator, the gift of its Lord, and the firmness of the commandment. Foreseeing, in its subjection, the freedom to fall [?], it would then wish to use that very freedom only to choose the service by which it would be ruled. Judged worthy, it would earn protection from its prudent service and a reward from its free will, as the apostle confirms when he says: "For if I do this willingly, I have a reward."

"Let there be two great lights," almighty God said, and they were made. He commanded them to divide day from night and to serve as signs and for seasons, days and years. Does not this division, once decreed, remain to this very day? And yet the Creator had the power to change these very things, which move in such ordered motion, whenever he willed, were he not held back by reason; for in all things God's power is joined to reason. If the Creator changed his works, how could the creature be expected to observe his commandments?

God commanded the earth to sprout grass, herbs and fruit-bearing trees. This it keeps even now, in the yearly round, bearing without ceasing. Yet God in his anger has very often reduced the fruits of the earth by withholding abundant rains. What he could have taken away entirely he chose rather to chastise, so that the blow might show correction and nature might keep its order.

God made man from the slime of the earth and, once he was alive by the breathing-in of the spirit of life, placed him in the paradise of delights. He also endowed him with free will and bound him with a commandment set between immortality and death. Yet those who have sucked the richer poisons from your breast assert that he was made mortal, and that the transgression of the commandment did him no harm. But in fact, when man transgressed, the earth is cursed. Man himself is burdened with labours and pains and is commanded to earn his bread in the sweat of his face. He is marked out for death until he returns to the earth from which he was taken. Adam is cast out of paradise and begets sons who carry with them the original sin of an unfaithful seed. The human race sins, and God himself repented that he had made man on the earth.

O Lord, bear with my foolishness a little while, until he who thinks himself wise and prudent blushes and recognizes his own imprudence! When one man sinned, and from him dreadful contagion passed into all his posterity and the reign of death grew strong over all, you repent, you are angry, you grieve, and you are moved, until the Word made flesh must undergo suffering, the cross and death.

Perhaps it would have been better for the one sinner to be destroyed at once and for another to be put in his place soon after by a second fashioning, so that a race free from all filth and unstained might descend from him. Or, almighty God, since we acknowledge that you did not do this, are we to believe that you could not?

O Peter, the rock on which Christ founded his Church, and O Paul, who laid the foundation other than which no one can lay, which is Christ: blessed apostles, pillars and bulwarks of the truth, at least you answer with your sacred words this man who sets himself up as God's counselor and mediator! Peter says:

"Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who in his great mercy has given you new birth into the hope of life through the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ from the dead, into an inheritance incorruptible and undefiled, kept in heaven for us, who are guarded by the power of God through faith for a salvation ready to be revealed in the last time."

Then Paul, the chosen vessel, brings out the treasures of salvation and says: "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ, even as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless in his sight in love; in which he predestined us to adoption as sons through Jesus Christ to himself, according to the purpose of his will, to the praise of his glory, in which he has favored us in the Beloved, in whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace, which he made to abound in us in all wisdom and prudence, making known to us the mystery of his will according to his good pleasure, which he purposed in him for the dispensation of the fullness of times: to restore all things in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth."

Peter says, "a salvation ready to be revealed in the last time"; Paul too testifies that God purposed in him, for the dispensation of the fullness of times, to restore all things in Christ. And now someone or other emerges before us like a frog out of the mud and croaks: "What need have I to wait for a time, to wait for judgment? If God can, he can always; if he can always, he is no respecter of persons!"

He can, then, and he can now; but in your case he would truly be proved a respecter of persons if what he can do in all, and will certainly do in his own time, he did in you alone before the time. He did not do it even in Moses, whom he reproached for only one sin in this life and yet forgave before his death, but whom on account of this fault he commanded to die, so that he did not enter the promised land.

Let him hear, then, Solomon bearing witness about the ordering of times and God's appointment: "All things have their time, and everything under heaven passes in its own season: a time to be born and a time to die; a time to plant and a time to uproot what has been planted; a time to kill and a time to heal." Then in another place he says:

"I saw under the sun, in the place of judgment, wickedness, and in the place of justice, iniquity; and I said in my heart: God will judge the righteous and the wicked, and then there will be a time for every matter."

Therefore, you empty man, if you have any confidence, wait patiently for God's ordering, which the Lord himself who made it deigned to wait for: he who had made the law was made under the law. Hear him saying to you: "It is not for you to know the times which the Father has set by his own authority."

Or, if you want to receive clearer testimony that, although God certainly can, he nevertheless does not act, for the sake of his own ordering, he says to Peter: "Do you think that I cannot ask my Father even now, and he will provide me with more than twelve legions of angels? But how then will the Scriptures be fulfilled, that it must happen thus?"

You see, then, that the one who works out time tempers his powers, and the principle of his dispensation mixes patience with might. Then the Lord says: "Put your sword back into its sheath. For it cannot be that I should not drink the cup which the Father has given me."

And yet there is nothing God cannot do, nor is there anything he does not do, except perhaps what he does not will, what is not fitting, what he does not purpose. Paul speaks to the Thessalonians, referring to the coming of the Antichrist: "Do you not remember that when I was still with you I told you these things? And now you know what restrains him, so that he may be revealed in his own time."

So great is the force of God's decree, and so irreversible the fixed order of the times appointed each for its own purposes, that the Lord said that for the sake of his elect the days of the world would be shortened, not taken away: so that he might give the appointed times their fullness in keeping with his majesty and their brevity in keeping with his mercy, and so that at the same time mercy might gain its shortening and the world might complete its number.

And you now — see, I speak with the grief of compassion — you, I say, O man like myself, want men to answer you that in this present time someone is without sin, a thing that is nowhere found said before in the sacred books; and, if perhaps they agreed to this, to put their signatures to the very day and moment,

building a new engine of slander, so that, when we say a thing does not happen, we may seem to have said it cannot happen, and in the very matter in which we above all proclaim God's omnipotence at work in the dispensation he has established, we may be judged impatiently to accuse him of impotence? Cast off this empty fury, I beg you, since this very thing only furthers sin; for in thinking about how sin is to be wiped away you seem to have considered the possibility of the time, not the clemency of the judge.

Let it suffice to have said this much about the power of God, which we proclaim and worship, and about the predetermination of the times, which have been fixed by his most profound counsel. Even if there were not the many writings of the saints on this point, the answer of the demons alone would be enough, who, condemned by their own conscience, cry out to the Lord: "What have you to do with us, Son of God? Why have you come before the time to destroy us?"

Since you understand that they are confessing the appointed time of judgment, take from it a most certain example against yourself. If you understand that they, though caught in the act of oppressing a wretched man, are condemned only then, at the last judgment, accept that you too are to be purged at that point by an unshakable cleansing; but if, as we read, God's patience still grants them free choice, believe that you too are still subject to temptation.

Now I pass briefly to another question, which you are said to brandish frequently against all Catholics. For even in that most elaborately worked letter of yours we could scarcely understand these very things. Did you, I say, a most modest man, not blush to write such things to Demetrias, a girl who, as I hear, is consecrated and holy — teaching, I suppose, reverence for chastity under the episode of Joseph and his lustful mistress — where you said: "Often spurned, the mistress lays closer snares for the youth; in private and without witnesses she shamelessly seizes him by the hand," weaving an unseemly story in most obscene language?

And yet we ought not to charge to you what is said neither aptly nor decently — you, whose birth did not grant you an education in more honorable studies, nor whose nature made you wise — but to those ghostwriters of yours, who set down a wretched idea in the most wretched language and expose you to be read with guffaws, as if you were a placard of shame.

Among these things, then, in that same letter you belched out in undigested language the claim that many of our people say that God created the nature of man evil. That Phinehas of yours also tried, step by step, to press this on us. On this I shall briefly first make my profession and then reply.

Let him not be worthy to stand at the right hand before the judgment seat of Christ among the lambs of God, nor deserve to see the Lord in the land of the living, nor may the life of Jesus be manifested in his mortal body in the glory of the resurrection, who says that God created any nature evil, whether of man or of anything else, or who takes away free choice in anyone, since he has read the words: "All the things that God made were very good."

And concerning man's free choice it is written: "God created man indestructible and left him in the hand of his own counsel." You blind and malicious man — for I cannot speak to you otherwise, since you have no sense of the Lord's authority, no sense of your own frailty, no sense of common understanding — we say that human nature is weak, not evil. For if it were evil, it could not receive the good at all; but since in fact it longs for the good with a natural desire, clings to the good, and utterly flees evil, where in it can one say there is an evil substance?

The Lord cries out: "The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak." Abraham cries out: "But I am dust and ashes." Job cries out: "Man is rottenness, and the son of man a worm." Isaiah cries out: "O wretched me, for I am pierced with sorrow, because I am a man and have unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people that has unclean lips."

Jeremiah cries out: "The soul in distress and the anxious spirit cry out to you: see, Lord, and have mercy." Habakkuk cries out: "I kept watch over myself, and my belly trembled at the voice of prayers, and my whole frame was troubled within me." David cries out: "Hear me in your righteousness, and do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no one living will be justified in your sight."

All the apostles, shaken by fear in their weakness, cry out: "Lord, save us, we are perishing." John cries out: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us." James cries out: "For in many things we all offend."

Paul cries out: "Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord." And so that the weakness of all might cry out in general, the Holy Spirit cries out in the saints: "All flesh is grass, and the glory of man like the flower of grass. The grass withers, the flower falls; but the word of the Lord endures forever."

Against these clouds of divine testimonies, so splendid and so clear, let the whole world, laboring in its groaning, hear Pelagius shouting back and resisting humble truth not only with impudent words but also with the branding irons of his writings.

For he says in the letter we named above: "But on the contrary, with slack and disdainful mind, like proud and worthless slaves, we shout back in the Lord's face and say: 'It is hard, it is difficult, we cannot; we are men, we are clothed in frail flesh.' And — O blind madness! O profane rashness! — we accuse the Lord of knowledge of a double ignorance, so that he seems not to know what he made and not to know what he commanded, and, as if he had forgotten human frailty, of which he himself is the author, to have laid on man what he cannot bear. What, I ask, could be more deadly than this presumption?

What more perverse than this reproach?" You upbraid the Catholic Church, whose very inward parts we are, as if in despair it seemed to say that God, the author of man, laid on man what he cannot bear;

yet her profession, both in her words and in her humility, is most faithful: that God at first commanded all things as possible, and then, since no one fulfilled what was possible — for which reason the whole world became subject to God — afterwards lightened the weight of the commandment by substituting the indulgence of grace.

But you, wicked and malicious servant, who try to exact from your fellow servants what your lord has forgiven you: I shall first examine your view, and afterwards, if it seems good, I shall set out my own.

You who charge some with having said that the burden of the law cannot be borne — are you then confident that you yourself can bear it? O wretched man, who, as it is written, say in your heart: "I am rich, I have grown rich, and I need nothing," and do not know that you are wretched and pitiable and poor and blind and naked.

Did Christ say to you, "Truly I tell you, flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven"? Did he say to you, "You shall be called Cephas"? Did he promise you, "On this rock I will build my Church"?

For consider what the apostle Peter, taught by the Holy Spirit, warns, when he says: "Now therefore, why do you test God by putting on the necks of the disciples a yoke which neither our fathers nor we ourselves have been able to bear? But we believe that we are saved through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, just as they are."

The apostle Peter says that the one who truly tests God is he who now tries to lay the burden of the law on man; but you, on the contrary, object and threaten that the one who accuses God of injustice is he who, by confessing his own weakness, flees from the letter that kills to the grace of the Spirit.

Samuel, Elijah, Elisha, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel, Zechariah — all the holy men, whether judges or kings or prophets, are without doubt our fathers; and Peter affirms that none of the fathers, nor indeed they themselves, that is, the apostles, though they were Jews, were able to bear the burden of the law, but that they were saved by faith in Christ according to the hope of grace.

Or perhaps, in your view, all these holy fathers did not have God's help? See, Peter rebukes those who were trying to put a heavy yoke on the necks of the disciples; you, on the contrary, to Peter's offense, rebuke those who flee to God's faithful mercy and do not trust that they can bear the burden of the law by themselves.
