But perhaps you have a special confidence in carrying burdens because, nourished by baths and banquets, you carry broad shoulders and a sturdy neck, displaying fat even on your forehead, as it is written: "For he has stretched out his hand against God and has made himself strong against the Almighty. He has run against him with neck held high and is armed with a fat neck. Fatness has covered his face, and lard hangs from his sides."

But those cannot be like this to whom Christ always speaks in the heart: "Strive to enter by the narrow way; for broad is the way that leads to death." And the apostle Paul warns: "Make no provision for the flesh in its desires." The truth of Christ is in me, for I grieve greatly for you. For, in the judgment of my blessed father Augustine, this is the confidence not of the sound but of the insane.

Let me question you, if you will deign to answer, about one commandment, and that the first. In the law the Lord commands through Moses, and Christ affirms it in the Gospels: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength"; and the second is like it: "You shall love your neighbor as yourself."

I ask you — answer not me but God, not with your voice but with your conscience — whether you love God with your whole heart in such a way that you never admit into it any thought that could be conceived apart from the fear and love of God; whether you follow him with your whole soul in such a way that, having once taken up the cross, you never yield to any delight at all when some pleasure offers itself for a time; whether you burn with the heat of charity in all your inmost being in such a way that you never give in at all to lusts or desires through the weak pleas of necessity;

and next, since it is written, "Whatever is not of faith is sin," whether, when you see bishops of illustrious sees, or powerful men of the world, or rich men under the profession of religion, you never concede anything at all, captured by flattery or fear or hope through respect of persons, nor anything for which your heart reproaches you and your conscience gnaws at you; or whether you never give answers suited to the occasion rather than to the truth.

This too I ask: do you love all Christians equally, as yourself? For under one head, which is Christ, and in one Church, which is Christ's, we are all brothers and one body in Christ. Confess, then, whether you love as yourself all who hope in God's mercy — those, that is, whom you know; for I am not asking about strangers, whom you suppose you love simply because, not knowing them, you do not hate them.

But why do I demand these things from your confession, when the common people know your way of life? You, perfect without weakness; you, able to bear the whole load of the law; you, I say, puffed-up but empty man, hear, if you will deign to, the Lord and Savior calling you back to holy things, if indeed you are able: "Truly I tell you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like an infant will not enter it."

An infant has nothing in itself except that it loves whoever caresses it, and that, hoping for its bread not by its own sweat but by its pleas, it obtains the nourishment of life by simple asking, which it does not earn by confident labor. Admonished by this comparison, turn back to infancy, so that you may return to life.
And since I said above concerning the possibility of bearing the burden, "I shall first examine your view, and afterwards, if it seems good, I shall set out my own":
my view is that we sin in this too, when, being weak, we complain of our weakness, as the apostle says: "Does the thing formed say to the one who formed it, 'Why have you made me thus'?"

For complaining of weakness is ambition for one's own strength, since whoever seeks a strength of his own secretly disdains the help of God. And this is the devil, who says, "I will do it by my strength." But I, following the apostle, will glory always in my weaknesses, so that my heart may always say to God: "In the shelter of your wings I will rejoice; my soul has clung to you; your right hand has upheld me."

Hence it is also written: "Let your requests be made known before God, and the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and bodies in Christ Jesus." So I have weakness, and I rejoice in the knowledge of my weakness. For when I am weak, then I am strong, by calling on the mighty God, who hears me in my weakness and who has most faithfully promised us: "And I am with you always, to the end of the age."

The proper work of weakness is to pray always and in every place, so that almighty God, who promised not to abandon us, may also never cease to help. For see, Scripture cries out to the weak: "Seek the Lord and be strengthened; seek his face always"; and a devout and true confession answers it: "Behold, as the eyes of servants are on the hands of their masters, so our eyes are on the Lord our God, until he has mercy on us."

Great and sure is our confidence of perfection when the Almighty does what the lowest desires; and again, great and sure is our security of being upheld when the Almighty keeps the weak and does not lose them; as it is written: "Now to him who is able to do all things more abundantly than we ask or understand, according to the power that is at work in us — to him be glory in Christ Jesus." Therefore

the apostle admonishes: "Set your minds on things above, not on things on earth; for you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, your life, appears, then you too will appear with him in glory." The fruit of life is holiness, and holiness is to be without sin. If, then, the glory of incorruption is hidden from all men in this time, how do you boast that in this same time you can be clothed with that very incorruption?

For just as the beginning of corruption for man was to turn aside into sin, so the beginning of incorruption will be to have no sin. Who, then, has drawn it out of its hiding place before God's judgment, or taken it from Christ's bosom and handed it to you? Or is it perhaps because you understand that you would not merit it in the future from the Lord's hand?

Paul instructs those who presume such things and says: "But when this mortal has put on immortality, then the saying that is written will come to pass: Death is swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting? Now the sting of death is sin."

By this the apostle shows that no one can in any way triumph over death and sin until immortality follows upon mortality and incorruption upon corruption, and when, weakness being abolished, perfect strength takes its place, when there will be neither male nor female, but all will be like the angels of God.

Now if anyone has already grown to such a height of holiness that, while living in this flesh, he does not know whether he is male or female; if, having already attained his own fullest purity and having no soiled garments, he is like the angels of God; and if he is already surrounded with that brightness, like the sun, which has been promised to the saints — then let him rightly profess this perfection not by his voice but by his condition.

Yet such presumption is ruin. Rather, it is better for such a man to listen not to his own heart but to Paul, the teacher of the Gentiles, and to follow him, and at the same time to pray with him, so that the Lord may answer him as he prays: "My grace is sufficient for you; for strength is made perfect in weakness."

Therefore, in the one thing in which alone free will is of use, let each of us offer himself to God as willing soil, for we are God's field; we are God's building. Let him cast the seed, the word, into his own field; let it be believed in the heart; let him plant, let him water, let him make fruitful, let him give the increase, for he is the true husbandman.

Yet in the one thing that willing devotion can do in us, let it faithfully supply what is needed to hold the root of the seed within itself and to nourish an abundant yield, and let it constantly rouse its husbandman with its prayers, so that the enemy cannot sow tares on top. Let this be its cooperation in God's work, with undoubting hope and sincere love.

For the Lord Jesus says: I am the vine, you are the branches. Whatever the branch has, it has from the vine. For, says the apostle, it is not you that support the root, but the root supports you. Why then does the branch exalt itself over the fruit that is seen on it, when everything belongs to the vine, not only its power to bear but its very existence? Otherwise it will be cut off and thrown into the fire. For it is not the branch but the vine that has the power, and what the vine can do, the branch displays.

It is enough, then, for each one to have; but from where and in whom he has it, let him both humbly acknowledge and patiently wait, lest, while he does not have and believes that he has, even what he has be taken away from him. God cast out of paradise the first man who sinned; then Christ led into paradise the first man who believed on the cross.

Rightly, then, so long as I am not in paradise and remain in the land of Adam's exile, I do not believe that I am without sin. But if by the grace of God I am brought across into paradise, there, my perfection attained, death overcome and sin blotted out, I shall proclaim the eternal glory of his power in the sight of God.

These things, most blessed bishops, I have set out as best I could, for the sake of faith and simplicity. Let those who have done harm not be angry with me if in any point they are designated by comparison with names. As for the questions, let them bear it with equanimity, and rather, if they have the fear of God, let them rejoice that what is true has been given as the answer.

With Jesus Christ as my witness, I confess that I hate the heresy, not the heretic; but, as is just, for the time being I avoid the heretic because of the heresy, since I have both tested and rebuked him. Let him detest and condemn it, by mouth and by hand alike, and he will be joined to all in the bond of brotherhood, for it is written: Bear one another's burdens, and so you will fulfil the law of Christ.
